title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. L is a totally ordered set, a 'tronçon', which may or may not have a smallest element α(L) and a largest element ω(L). In the chapter this order-theoretic material is the 1-dimensional groundwork for 'réseaux via découpages', i.e. networks or graphs obtained by cutting things into tame pieces.

What the previous page settled. Page 23 tried a coarser topology in which both ]a,b[ and [a,b] would be open. It found that the hoped-for closure formulas, such as closure(]a,b[) = [a,b], fail.

Decision on this page.
- Grothendieck goes back to the topology defined first, essentially the order topology. He notes it is well behaved with respect to the 'intervalles' or 'intersections' (the word is unclear).
- By abuse of language he calls the following 'closed' softened (or bi-softened) sub-tronçons ('sous-tronçons adoucis / biadoucis fermés'): [a,b], L_{≤a}, L_{≥a}, and L itself.
- These are assumed not reduced to a point: a<b for [a,b], a ≠ α(L) for L_{≤a}, a ≠ ω(L) for L_{≥a}.
- A 'large' closed sub-tronçon is then either such a sub-tronçon or a single point.

Boundary. For such T he starts to define the 'absolute boundary' ∂T as the finite set of its extremities, with card ∂T ∈ {0,1,2}. The crossed-out examples are ∂[a,b]={a,b}, ∂L_{≤a}=∂L_{≥a}={a}, ∂L=∅.

All of this is struck out and redone on page 25. There ∂T is the set of smallest and largest elements of T, and he proves ∂T = (Fr T ∩ T) ⊔ (T ∩ ∂L). Page 25 then defines 'tranches' as T minus a subset of ∂T, which gives the half-open and open intervals.

Purpose. This is bookkeeping for the closed and half-open 1-cells (edges with or without endpoints) of a combinatorial or tame-topological theory of networks.
errors: The crossed-out claim ∂L = ∅ holds only if L has no smallest or largest element. With the definition 'extremities of T', ∂L consists of α(L) and/or ω(L) when they exist. Grothendieck evidently noticed this: page 25 writes '∂L = ∂L (sic)' and uses T ∩ ∂L in the boxed formula.
The examples ∂L_{≤a} = ∂L_{≥a} = {a} likewise ignore that L_{≤a} also contains α(L) if it exists. Then ∂L_{≤a} = {α(L), a}, so the stated values hold only when L has no extremities.

ideas.what: Closed intervals and closed rays of a totally ordered set, with points as degenerate cases ('sous-tronçons fermés')
ideas.modern_name: closed intervals / convex closed subsets in an order topology

ideas.what: Absolute boundary of an interval as its set of extremities, with cardinality 0, 1 or 2, related to the topological frontier via ∂T = (Fr T ∩ T) ⊔ (T ∩ ∂L) (formula on the next page)
ideas.modern_name: endpoints of an interval; manifold-with-boundary boundary in dimension 1

deep.surprise_reason: These are elementary definitions about intervals in a totally ordered set, mostly crossed out and redone on the following page. The material is only notable as groundwork for the 1986 'réseaux via découpages' project. Nothing here is new mathematics.
transcription_corrections: The smallest and largest elements are written α(L) and ω(L): read 'a ≠ α(L) resp. a ≠ ω(L)', not 'a≠or(L)' / 'a≠ex(L)'. This matches 'a≠α' / 'a≠σ' on page 25, which should likewise read α(L) and ω(L).
'Un sous-tronçon fermé large' (or with 'large' struck out) rather than 'long'.
The parenthetical may read 'bien fermée sous les "intersections"' rather than '"intervalles"'. The reading is uncertain.
'minimaux[?]' is probably not present; the sentence reads 'on appellera, par abus de langage, les [a,b], L_{≤a}, L_{≥a} (ainsi que L) sous-tronçons adoucis (ou biadoucis) "fermés"'.
